Design concept · W-band FMCW radar · October 2026

W-band Radar Platform

A W-band FMCW radar in a round CCTV-style housing: two 8 × 12 antenna-in-package arrays for transmit and receive with the chirp synthesizer on the same board, a 4-channel X-band dechirp and digitising board built around the NXP LA1214, an NXP i.MX 95 for processing and Ethernet, and a power board for all of it. The hard problems are band alignment between the chips and the array, and transmit-to-receive isolation — not the beamforming.

01 · Concept

What we are building

A W-band FMCW radar on four round boards in one aluminium tube: the antennas and the chirp synthesizer at the front, then the X-band dechirp and digitiser, the processor, and the power supply, with every cable leaving through the rear cap.

RF: X-band IF and LO between the discs, W-band over the air digital data: PCIe, Ethernet power: 12 V bus and DC input
2 × 96antenna-in-package tiles, TX + RX, 8 × 12 each at 3.30 mm pitch
29.0 dBiboresight gain at 95 GHz, beam 4.0° × 6.0° (full-wave CST)
95–99.9 GHzusable band of the 8 × 12 array (active match)
4 channelscomplex, one per RX quadrant, into the LA1214
i.MX 95processing on the unit; Ethernet + PoE++ out
Ø127 mmaluminium tube, ≈ 61 W input at the nominal load

The front board carries two identical 8 × 12 tile arrays side by side, one for transmit and one for receive, with a 5 mm gap between them. Each tile is a 3.30 × 3.30 mm package with a 2 × 2 patch antenna on top and a W-band CMOS IC underneath. The TX IC multiplies an X-band drive by 9. The RX IC mixes the echo with 8 times the same drive. One ramp synthesizer on the back of the same board makes that drive.

The receive array is split into four 24-tile quadrants. Each quadrant is combined at X-band and sent down to the second board as one channel. There, two LMS8001 shift the four channels to I/Q baseband and the LA1214 digitises them, runs the range FFT and forms the sum and difference beams. The i.MX 95 detects and tracks targets and sends the result out over Ethernet. The last board turns PoE++ or 24/48 V DC into the rails for all four.

Three things this page argues

  • inferenceOne chirp, one frequency plan. A single X-band chirp at 10.556–10.833 GHz drives the ×9 transmitters, the ×8 receive LO and the dechirp mixer. The receive IF then falls back into X-band, and the beat is the same as in a native W-band FMCW radar with 9 times the X-band slope. Section 04.
  • inferenceQuadrant monopulse with digital Σ and Δ. Four calibrated channels are enough to form Σ, ΔAZ, ΔEL and ΔΔ in software, the same beams the CST runs used. Full-wave CST gives a monopulse slope km of 1.42 in elevation and 1.46 in azimuth. Section 09.
  • openTwo problems are not solved yet. Band alignment: the array works at 95–99.9 GHz, the TX IC peaks at 94.5 GHz and the RX IC is best at 92–96 GHz, so the common band is only about 95–97.5 GHz. Isolation: the worst RX port sees −41.5 dB of TX coupling against a 65 dB requirement, 21.8–23.5 dB short at 95 GHz. Section 04, section 10.

02 · Concept

Why W-band

At 95 GHz a palm-sized aperture already gives a 4° × 6° beam and a few gigahertz of sweep give centimetre range bins; what it costs is weather loss, a wet window and very tight electrical lengths.

Compact apertureλ is 3.16 mm at 95 GHz. 96 tiles fit in 26.4 × 39.6 mm, and that aperture gives a 3.99° × 6.04° beam and 29.0 dBi.confirmed
High range resolutionΔR = c/2B. The 2.5 GHz baseline sweep gives 6.0 cm range bins; the 4.9 GHz wide mode gives 3.1 cm.inference
Electronic steeringEach tile IC sets its own phase, so the beam moves without moving parts. At 3.30 mm pitch the useful range is ±10°.confirmed
Edge processingRange FFT and Σ/Δ run in the LA1214, detection and tracking in the i.MX 95. In normal use only detections and tracks leave the unit.inference
3.16 mmwavelength at 95 GHz (3.07 mm at 97.5 GHz)
4.0° × 6.0°beam of the 26.4 × 39.6 mm aperture, elevation × azimuth
6.0 cmrange bin with 2.5 GHz of sweep (95.0–97.5 GHz)
3.1 cmrange bin with 4.9 GHz of sweep (95–99.9 GHz)
≈ 0.4 dB/kmclear-air absorption at sea level near 95 GHz

Same aperture, three bands

Keep the 26.4 × 39.6 mm aperture and change only the frequency. The beam widens as λ/D and the gain falls as λ².

BandλBeam el × azIdeal directivityEcho power
24 GHz12.49 mm16.1° × 24.1°19.3 dBi−12.0 dB
77 GHz3.89 mm5.0° × 7.5°29.4 dBi−1.8 dB
95 GHz (this unit)3.16 mm4.1° × 6.1°31.2 dBi0 dB (reference)

Beam ≈ 51°·λ/D; directivity = 4πA/λ²; echo power for the same aperture on TX and RX scales as A²/λ², relative to 95 GHz. Uniform aperture, no losses. inference At 95 GHz full-wave CST gives 3.99° × 6.04° and 29.0 dBi realised, so the estimate holds within 0.1° and the 2.2 dB gap is mostly the 63 % total efficiency (−2.0 dB).

This is what makes the round housing possible. Both apertures and the 5 mm gap fit on a 64.5 × 46.3 mm ground plate, which sits inside a Ø110 mm disc with room for clamp rings and mounting holes. At 24 GHz the same aperture would give a 16° × 24° beam; at 77 GHz it would give 5.0° × 7.5° and 1.8 dB less echo power.

Clear air is not the problem at the ranges this unit sees. At 150 m the two-way path is 0.3 km, so 0.4 dB/km costs about 0.12 dB. Rain, a wet window and the tolerances below matter far more.

What W-band costs
  • inferenceRain. Specific attenuation near 95 GHz is of order 5 dB/km at 10 mm/h (ITU-R P.838 order of magnitude). That is about 1.5 dB two-way at 150 m, and more in heavy rain. It sets the range margin in bad weather, not the clear-air number.
  • openWater film and ice on the window. A wet radome absorbs and reflects at a 3 mm wavelength. The plan is a hydrophobic coating and a heated bezel ring; any heater wire across the aperture must run perpendicular to the E-field, and the polarisation is not stated yet. The loss has to be measured.
  • inferenceTight electrical lengths. The TX IC multiplies by 9, so an X-band delay error acts as the same delay at W-band. 0.05 mm of stripline (0.29 ps) is already 10° at 97 GHz. Static errors can be calibrated with the IC phase control, but 1 mm of mismatch adds about 10° across a 4.9 GHz chirp that calibration cannot remove. All 96 LO paths per array stay equal within about 1 mm.
  • confirmedLow power per chip. The simulated TX IC output peaks at about +1.6 dBm; the RX IC noise figure is 6–7 dB at 92–96 GHz. The array supplies the rest: 96 tiles give about 50 dBm EIRP at 95 GHz boresight (our sum of simulated IC output, +19.8 dB array power and 29.0 dBi).
  • confirmedPitch close to λ. 3.30 mm equals λ at 90.85 GHz. Together with a tile-cell resonance near 90.6 GHz this rules out 85–94.4 GHz and leaves 95–99.9 GHz as the usable band. See section 07.
  • inferenceThin, accurate radome. A half-wave polycarbonate wall at 97.5 GHz is only 0.92 mm thick. Its reflection stays at or below −27 dB over 95–99.9 GHz, but only if the thickness is held. See section 19.
03 · Concept

One signal chain on four round boards

One synthesizer on the W-band disc makes the chirp for transmit, receive LO and dechirp; the RX array leaves that disc as four X-band channels, which the X-band disc turns into digital Σ and Δ beams for the processor.

RF: chirp, LO trees, IF, I/Q baseband reference clocks control: SPI, ROW/COL, ramp trigger digital data: PCIe, Ethernet power

Follow the orange lines. The synthesizer sweeps 10.556–10.833 GHz in the baseline mode. One output feeds the two LO trees, which bring about +6.6 dBm to each of the 192 tiles. The TX ICs multiply by 9 and radiate 95.0–97.5 GHz. The RX ICs mix the echo with 8 times the same drive, so each RX tile puts out an IF in the X-band again. Each quadrant of 24 tiles is summed at that IF and sent down on one SMPM.

The second synthesizer output goes down as the dechirp LO. On the X-band disc a 90° hybrid splits it into 0° and 90° for the two LMS8001, which become the I and Q halves of one 4-channel mixer. The LA1214 digitises the four I/Q pairs, does the range FFT and forms Σ, ΔAZ and ΔEL. Besides RF and power, only PCIe data, one reference and a few control lines cross between the boards. inference

04 · Concept

Frequency plan: ×9 out, ×8 in

One X-band chirp is multiplied by 9 for transmit and by 8 for the receive LO, so the receive IF lands back in the X-band, and mixing it with the same chirp leaves exactly the beat of a W-band FMCW radar.

RF chirp, LO, IF delayed copy or reference ramp axes, beat
×9 / ×8multiplication in the TX IC / for the RX LO, from one drive
10.556–10.833GHz X-band sweep for the baseline; BX 278 MHz
6.0 cmrange bin of the baseline, BW 2.5 GHz
3.06 cmrange bin of the wide mode, BW 4.9 GHz
95–97.5 GHzwhere array, TX IC and RX IC all work

The algebra

  • Transmit: 9·fX(t). Echo: 9·fX(t − τ). RX LO: 8·fX(t). With a linear chirp of slope SX, fX(t − τ) = fX(t) − SX·τ.
  • IF = 9·fX(t − τ) − 8·fX(t) = fX(t) − 9·SX·τ. The IF is the X-band chirp itself, offset by the beat.
  • Dechirp with fX(t): beat = 9·SX·τ = SW·τ. This is a native W-band FMCW with slope SW = 9·SX and sweep BW = 9·BX.
  • Phase noise: 9·φ(t − τ) − 8·φ(t) − φ(t) = 9·[φ(t − τ) − φ(t)]. It cancels at short range, but only if one synthesizer feeds the TX drive, the RX LO and the dechirp LO through matched paths. inference
W-bandfX = f/9RX LO = 8·fXIF at zero rangeNoteStatus

97.5 GHz10.833 GHz86.67 GHz10.833 GHztop of the baseline chirpinference
99.9 GHz11.100 GHz88.80 GHz11.100 GHztop of the usable band; the TX IC LO input is specified to 11 GHz (99 GHz)open
85.5–94.5 GHz9.50–10.50 GHz76.0–84.0 GHz9.50–10.50 GHzold deck chirp: below the usable band, so the X-band sweep moves up by about 1 GHzconfirmed

Band alignment

array usable band array unusable TX IC output RX IC conversion gain RX tile V1 gain

Each block has its own best band, and they do not line up. The 8 × 12 array matches only from 95 to 99.9 GHz. The TX IC is strongest at 94.5 GHz and has lost 4.3 dB by 97.7 GHz. The RX IC is best at 92–96 GHz: its noise figure is 6–7 dB there and about 8 dB at 98 GHz. The earlier RX tile V1 peaks at 92 GHz and is not the tile in the CST array. TX and RX IC curves were read from plots. confirmed

Baseline chirp 95.0–97.5 GHz: fX 10.556–10.833 GHz, BX 278 MHz, BW 2.5 GHz, ΔR 6.0 cm, where the array, the TX IC and the RX IC all work. Wide mode 95–99.9 GHz: BX 544 MHz, BW 4.9 GHz, ΔR 3.06 cm, at lower TX power and RX gain. TX and RX ICs centred 2–3 GHz higher would remove the compromise. inference

Delays, leakage and the IC limits
  • inferencePath delays set a zero-range offset. With X-band line delays τT to the TX tile, τR to the RX LO, τI on the IF return and τL on the LO copy, the beat becomes SX·(9τ + 9τT − 8τR + τI − τL). The range offset is (c/2)·(9τT − 8τR + τI − τL)/9: 1.7 cm with all four delays at 1 ns, and 10 cm with 1.5 / 1 / 1 / 0.5 ns. Calibrate it out on a corner reflector.
  • inferenceLO → IF leakage lands at DC. The IF band is the drive band, 10.56–11.1 GHz. Any X-band drive that leaks into the IF lines mixes down to near-zero beat. The X-band disc needs a high-pass after the mixer, and the W-band disc keeps LO and IF on separate stripline layers behind via fences.
  • inferenceMatched paths also protect against TX → RX leakage. The −41.5 dB coupling tone sits at near-zero range. Its ×9 phase noise is cancelled only as far as the delays match. See section 10.
  • openTX IC above 99 GHz. The TX IC LO input is specified at 10–11 GHz. The wide mode needs 11.1 GHz for 99.9 GHz, 0.1 GHz beyond that.
  • openTX IC bandwidth label. The TX IC plot carries a "7 GHz 3-dB BW" label, but its markers sit 5.6 GHz apart at W-band and 4.35 dB below the peak. The plotted quantity or the multiplication factor needs a check with the IC designer.
  • inferenceRX IC compression. The measured IP1dB is −17 to −21 dBm at IF 10–13 GHz, so the ≈ −40 dBm of TX leakage per RX tile stays about 20 dB below compression.
  • inferenceWhy not a DAC chirp. The LA1214 TX DACs could make the chirp, but NXP rates the channel below 140 MHz. That is 1.26 GHz at W-band and 11.9 cm range bins. The DACs stay for calibration tones, BIST and waveform experiments; see section 12.
05 · W-band layer

W-band board: two apertures and the synthesizer

One Ø110 mm board carries both apertures on its front and the whole X-band side of the W-band layer on its back: the chirp synthesizer in the middle, two LO trees, four IF outputs and the beam-control CPLD.

tile, 3.30 mm, four patches X-band LO and IF 1:12 column trees on inner layers reference in beam control, ROW/COL select 1.2 V POLs, fed with 12 V over the header
192tiles: 96 TX + 96 RX, 8 × 12 each at 3.30 mm
1synthesizer (LMX2595) for the TX drive, the RX LO and the dechirp LO
18LO amplifiers: 2 roots + 16 column drivers
+6.6 dBmLO at every tile, 1.6 dB over the ≈ +5 dBm the TX IC needs
4IF outputs at X-band, one per RX quadrant, on SMPM
≈ 35–55 Won this disc, ≈ 25 A at 1.2 V (inference)

Everything on the front is set by the CST model: two 26.4 × 39.6 mm apertures centred 15.7 mm left and right of the axis, 5.0 mm apart at the tile edges, on one 64.5 × 46.3 mm ground plate confirmed. The plate's corners reach r = 39.7 mm, so a Ø110 mm disc leaves a 24 mm segment above and below the plate and 15 mm side lenses for parts. The back is a placement proposal inference: the synthesizer sits on the axis so both trees start with equal lengths, and the four IF jacks sit at the quadrant centres so each one drops straight down to the X-band disc.

LO distribution: two stages of gain per tree

Each TX IC wants about +5 dBm of X-band drive at 10–11 GHz confirmed. A passive 96-way tree loses about 26 dB, so the synthesizer would have to deliver +31 dBm. Each tree therefore has a root amplifier, an equal-length 1:8 splitter, eight column drivers and a 1:12 stripline tree under every column. Both amplifier stages run 4 dB below P1dB, and every tile gets +6.6 dBm.

Levels are planning numbers for HMC441-class roots and HMC1082-class drivers inference. The RX IC's LO need is not specified; the RX tree assumes the TX number open.

Four RX quadrants, four IF channels

The RX tiles mix down on the tile, so the receive array is combined at X-band IF, not at W-band. Each 24-tile quadrant has its own 24:1 combiner, IF LNA and SMPM jack. The X-band disc digitises the four channels and forms the sum and the three difference beams in software, the same beams the CST monopulse runs used (section 09).

  • inferencePhase matching. The tiles multiply the drive by 9 (TX) and 8 (RX), so an X-band delay error acts like the same delay at W-band: 0.05 mm of stripline is already 10° at 97 GHz. The IC phase control calibrates static errors. A length error also turns into a phase slope across the chirp, about 10° per mm over 4.9 GHz, which calibration at one frequency cannot remove. Keep all 96 paths of each tree equal within ≈ 1 mm.
  • inferenceLO and IF share a band. The LO trees and the IF combiners both carry ≈ 10.6–11.1 GHz. They need separate stripline layers with via fences between them. What still leaks from LO to IF lands near DC after the dechirp, as a static offset.
  • inferenceBeam control. A CPLD on the back drives a shared CLK/D/RST bus plus 12 ROW and 8 COL select lines per array, matching the TX IC pins EN, RST, CLK, D, ROW, COL, ADDR(2:0), BIT(2:1). Beam tables are loaded over SPI from the X-band disc, and writes happen in the blank time between chirps.
  • openPhase bits. Neither IC's phase-bit count, register map or phase-shifter location is known. If the phase shifter sits on the X-band LO before the ×9, every X-band step becomes 9 steps at W-band.
  • openTile placement. The CST tiles touch at 3.30 mm. A real assembly needs 50–100 µm placement gaps or multi-tile packages (the TX module work used 2 × 2), and the BGA count per tile is not known.
Synthesizer options and the previous LO design

Chirp synthesizer

The baseline chirp is 10.556–10.833 GHz (95.0–97.5 GHz after ×9), and the wide mode goes to 11.100 GHz. RFoutA feeds the two LO trees, and RFoutB goes over a blind-mate SMPM to the X-band disc as the dechirp LO. The reference and the ramp trigger come up from the X-band disc, so the chirp starts on the same sample phase as the converters inference.

  • The LMX2595 must sweep the chirp without a VCO recalibration. A ramp that needs recalibration is limited to 250 kHz/µs, while 278 MHz in 100 µs is 2.8 MHz/µs. The VCO core boundaries near 10.5–11.1 GHz decide whether the baseline fits in one core open. If not, the ADF4159 with an external X-band VCO is the closest relative of the previous design.
  • The ×9 adds 19.1 dB of phase noise. Scaled from the 15 GHz figure, about −112.7 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz on 11 GHz becomes about −93.6 dBc/Hz at 99 GHz. Range correlation removes most of it for short paths, including the TX → RX leakage, but only if one synthesizer feeds all three paths inference.

What changed from the previous design

  • One PLL module fed eight RX boards and one TX board through cables. Now the synthesizer and both trees sit on the W-band board, next to the tiles.
  • The old RX branch delivered +5.5 dBm per board connector to boards with their own gain. The new per-tile ICs need ≈ +5 dBm each, 192 times, hence the second gain stage.
  • The old TX branch had a switch, a 0–45 dB step attenuator and a PA. Its labels do not add up: 22 dBm after the PA and +21 dBm after an 8-way splitter that loses about 10 dB. Do not reuse those numbers open.

  3. : four H-slots, a 0.50 × 0.10 mm bar with 0.10 × 0.20 mm end caps, one under each patch.
  4. : 75 µm, εr 3.25; the lower prepregs PP3 and PP4 (εr 3.1) are shown in the same colour.
  5. : two arms, four stubs that cross the slots and run 0.40 mm beyond them, and the trunk to the coax-like via.
  6. : a 0.90 × 0.80 mm window where the X-band LO crosses as three CPW lines.
  7. : LO GSG launch at the −x edge, RF output trace and the C-ring around the coax-like via; the two 100 Ω LO terminations of the CST model in amber.
  8. : 7 bumps on the RF pads (LO in and W-band out, both GSG) and 35 pads, 80 µm octagons on a 150 µm grid.
  9. : 1.80 × 1.20 × 0.28 mm, flip-chipped under the feed.
  10. : 48 perimeter vias (M5 to M1) and 25 cross vias (M3 to M1), 0.10 mm diameter.
  11. : the LO GSG balls at the −x edge and a DC and control row; the real ball map is not known.
  12. : the ground plane of the CST model, 5 µm below the IC back.

W-band board, Ø110 × 2.0 mm (front: tiles; back: LO, IF and control)

  1. : 96 tiles, 8 × 12 at 3.30 mm, centre x = −15.7 mm.
  2. : 96 tiles in four 24-tile quadrants (UL, UR, LL, LR), centre x = +15.7 mm; the Quadrants button tints them.
  3. : a 4 mm aluminium wall, 5 mm tall, in the 5 mm gap, with absorber on both faces.
  4. : under its 12 × 12 mm can at (0, +34) mm on the back.
  5. : root amplifier, equal-length 1:8 splitter and 8 column drivers; the 1:12 column trees run on inner layers.
  6. : the same, mirrored on the RX side.
  7. : four 24:1 combiners on inner layers, one X-band IF LNA at each quadrant output.
  8. : 4 IF out at (15.7 ± 6.6, ±9.9) mm, the dechirp LO out and the REF in beside the can.
  9. : at (0, −34) mm; ROW/COL select lines to both arrays, beam tables written between chirps.
  10. : four inductors and two controllers on the side lenses, close to the half-arrays.
  11. : 2 × 30 pins at (0, −40) mm for SPI, trigger, enable and 12 V.
  12. : four holes at r = 46 mm, 45°, and the bare rim where the clamp ring presses the board onto its spreader.

Tile stack-up

Six copper layers in 0.535 mm of low-loss laminate put the patches on top and the LO launch on the bottom; the W-band IC hangs underneath on seven bumps, inside the stand-off to the carrier board.

M1 patches, frame and cross copper layers and vias core and prepregs air layer of the CST model W-band IC bumps; BGA ball (dashed: assumed)

The antenna is aperture-coupled. Four 0.75 mm patches on M1 sit over H-shaped slots in the M3 ground. A 2 × 2 corporate feed on M4 crosses all four slots in the same direction, so the patches radiate in phase with E along y. The IC's output bump drives the feed through a coax-like via from M6 to M4. The X-band LO enters at the −x edge as a GSG launch on M6, dips through a window in the M5 ground and reaches the IC's input bumps. A grounded frame and cross on M1, with 48 + 25 fence vias, cage each patch.

Ports, terminations and model notes
  • confirmedPort 1, the antenna feed, is a 50 Ω discrete port at the IC's output bump, from the chip surface to the bump bottom. Every array keeps one per tile. Array build logs print tile centres; the real port sits 0.547 mm to the +x side and 0.021 mm up, at z ≈ −0.278 mm.
  • confirmedPort 2, the X-band LO, is a waveguide port on the −x face of the single tile (x = −1.65 mm, y ±0.55 mm). The arrays drop it, because it would sit inside the neighbouring tile. A tile-cell resonance near 90.6 GHz couples into this port; it is half of the 90 GHz problem in section 07.
  • confirmedTwo 100 Ω terminations sit between the LO input's S bump and each G bump. In parallel they load the LO pads with 50 Ω at the die. The arrays keep them: 192 per array, 384 in the TX + RX twin. In the RX tiles of the twin they absorb 1.6–3.2× the power that reaches the RX ports.
  • openThe 30 µm air layer. The model has nothing between the two upper prepregs, at z 0.175–0.205 mm. That is where the slotted ground used to be before it moved down 0.1 mm. A real laminate fills the gap with resin. Its effect on match and gain is not known; one tile run with prepreg there would settle it.
  • confirmedCST port numbering is not row-major. Ports 1–8 are row 0. After that the numbering runs up each column: port(i, 0) = 1 + i and port(i, j ≥ 1) = 9 + 11·i + (j − 1). So port 9 is tile (0, 1), port 20 is (1, 1) and port 96 is (7, 11). In the twin the RX ports are the TX ports + 96. Tile numbers on this page are row-major (8·j + i), mapped from the CST ports with that rule.
  • confirmedThe RX array in the twin is the TX tile, translated (not mirrored), with its ports terminated, so the RX tiles' LO edge faces the TX array. No CST array uses a real RX antenna-in-package.
  • inferencePads. Only the 7 RF pads have bumps in CST; the other 28 (DC, digital, ground) are bare. The right-hand pad column reaches x = 0.906 mm, just outside the 1.80 mm die, so the CST die block is slightly smaller than the real die, or offset from it.
  • openFeed details. The model history splits the M4 feed and deletes some pieces; the geometry used here keeps the whole shape, so chamfers and exact trace widths are approximate.
07 · W-band layer

Array performance from full-wave CST

One 8 × 12 aperture of 3.30 mm tiles, solved full-wave with all 96 ports driven, gives 29.0 dBi at 95 GHz; the band is usable from 95 to 99.9 GHz because the array breaks down near 90.7 GHz.

Why the band starts at 95 GHz

  • confirmedEvery tile is worse than −10 dB active match at 85–89.4 and 90.6–94.4 GHz, for every beam. At boresight the median tile is better than −10 dB from 94.9 to 99.9 GHz.
  • confirmedTwo effects meet near 90.7 GHz: a parasitic resonance of the 3.30 mm tile cell (≈ 90.6 GHz) and the pitch reaching one wavelength (90.85 GHz), where the boresight grating lobes enter along the array surface. The CST data do not separate them.
  • confirmedThe cost: 19.1 dBi at 90.5 GHz (14 % efficiency); at 90 GHz 63–69 % of the accepted power is lost in the structure, at 88 GHz 2.6 dB goes to mismatch.
  • inferenceThe chirp must stay at or above 95 GHz (frequency plan). The resonance follows the cell (f × pitch ≈ 299 GHz·mm): a 3.00 mm cell moves it to the 100 GHz edge, 2.90 mm to 103 GHz.
CST charts: gain, efficiency and active match
Details

Solver and model

  • CST time-domain (FIT) solver, hexahedral mesh, 85–100 GHz; far-field monitors at 88, 90, 95 and 98 GHz.
  • 8 × 12 model: 77.2 M mesh cells, 96 ports plus the tiles' 192 lumped elements; each tile's X-band edge port is removed.
  • Energy limit −20 dB for the scan runs, −30 dB for the gain-versus-frequency run. The two agree within 0.01 dB at 95–98 GHz; at 88 GHz they differ by 0.32 dB (25.9 dBi in the main run).
  • 27 beams: Σ, scan-plane Δ and cross-axis Δ at boresight, ±10° and ±20° in both planes. Port delays were checked to 0.005° before the solve.
  • About 34 min of matrix setup, then 1–1.2 h per beam and ≈ 50 GB of RAM on a 16-core laptop with 128 GB. The TX + RX twin (isolation) has 152 M cells and needs 1.6–2.2 h per beam.

08 · W-band layer

Scan range and grating lobes

The 3.30 mm pitch is 1.05–1.10 λ across the usable band, so every steered beam pulls a grating lobe into view: at ±10° it stays near −11 dB, at ±20° it is almost as strong as the beam.

The array factor of a uniform line repeats every λ/d in sin θ, so a second full-height lobe sits at sin θGL = sin θs − λ/d. Only the tile's own pattern holds it down. Steering moves the beam onto the tile pattern's flank and the grating lobe towards its centre, so the lobe grows quickly with scan angle and with frequency. CST cuts, 95 GHz

±10° works at 3.30 mm; ±20° does not. At 95 GHz the ±10° grating lobes are −10.7 to −13.6 dB, but only 95 GHz meets −10 dB at el −10° (−7.3 dB at 90 GHz, −6.2 dB at 98 GHz). At ±20° they reach −4.0 to −5.2 dB, and −1.1 dB at 98 GHz. The requirement is ±10° maximum. For margin over the whole band, use a 2.90–3.00 mm pitch or rotate neighbouring tiles in a checkerboard (pitch study below).

09 · W-band layer

Monopulse from four quadrants

The RX aperture is read out as four 24-tile quadrants on four X-band channels; the LA1214 forms Σ, ΔAZ, ΔEL and ΔΔ in software, and each detection's angle is Im(Δ/Σ) divided by the slope k.

W-band to X-band IF (analog)digital samples and beamsquadrant addedquadrant subtracted
1.42 / 1.46normalised slope km, el / az, 95 GHz (ideal aperture 1.39–1.43)
0.355 / 0.241slope k of Im(Δ/Σ) per degree, el / az
0.32° / 0.47°angle noise at SNR 16 dB, el / az, thermal only

29–56 dBΔ null depth below Σ, within 0.25° of the commanded angle

The CST beams are defined exactly as the quadrant sums: ΔEL is the upper six rows minus the lower six, ΔAZ the right four columns minus the left four. So the full-wave slopes and nulls apply to the digital beams directly, provided the four channels match. The beam shape is what an ideal uniform aperture gives; the tile adds nothing and costs nothing here.

Calibrate the four channels

An imbalance between the two halves of a Δ beam fills the null and, through its phase part, shifts the angle. Two degrees of phase already cost 0.05–0.07°, a quarter of the 0.2° requirement.

Imbalance (amplitude / phase)Δ null fillAngle bias, el / az
0.1 dB / 1°−39.6 dB0.02° / 0.04°
0.25 dB / 2°−32.9 dB0.05° / 0.07°
0.5 dB / 5°−25.6 dB0.12° / 0.18°
1 dB / 10°−19.6 dB0.25° / 0.36°

inference Two-half model, Δ/Σ = (1 − g·ejφ)/(1 + g·ejφ) at zero offset; bias = Im(Δ/Σ)/k. Target ≤ 0.25 dB / 2°, using the LA1214 TX DAC tone injected at the four IF inputs (X-band board).

The 0.2° at 16 dB requirement is not met by 8 × 12. Thermal noise alone gives 0.32° in elevation and 0.47° in azimuth. Meeting it at 16 dB needs about 1.6× the elevation and 2.35× the azimuth aperture: roughly 19 columns × 20 rows per array, so TX + RX side by side become ≈ 130 × 66 mm (146 mm diagonal). That does not fit a Ø110 mm disc; a Ø160 mm housing would take it. The other way out is more SNR at the angle measurement: ≥ 20.0 dB (el) and ≥ 23.3 dB (az). inference

Details

How the slope is measured

  • σθ = θ3 / (km·√(2·SNR)) = 1 / (k·√(2·SNR)), with k the slope of Im(Δ/Σ) per degree and km = k·θ3. Check: 3.99° / (1.416 × √79.6) = 0.32° at 16 dB.
  • Figures and stats: least-squares fit over ±¼ θ3 around the commanded angle, on co-polar complex 0.25° cuts. The negative scans use a linear fit over ±1° around the Δ null. The methods differ by 0.01–0.04 in km.
  • Over 88–98 GHz and 0/10/20° (24 cases): σθ at 16 dB is 0.31–0.37° (el) and 0.46–0.55° (az); 0.2° needs 19.7–21.3 dB (el) and 23.3–24.9 dB (az).
  • Cross-axis Δ beams (ΔAZ while steered in elevation and the reverse): km 1.38–1.43; the null sits 38.7–45.7 dB below the Σ peak at 95 GHz.

What the numbers leave out

  • confirmedThermal noise only, one measurement. Channel imbalance, calibration residuals and the quadrant combiners are not in the CST numbers.
  • confirmedFirst side lobes of Σ and Δ are equal (≈ −13 dB). 20–40° off the beam Δ is 4.6–7.6 dB above Σ.
  • inferenceSo a target in a Σ side lobe gives a wrong angle. Reject detections where |Δ| > |Σ|, and use ΔΔ as a cross-check: it stays near zero for a point target on the beam axis.
  • openMultipath, target glint and the radome's effect on the slope; the 24:1 combiner tolerance inside each quadrant.
10 · W-band layer

TX → RX isolation

With the two apertures 5 mm apart, full-wave CST puts the worst RX port at −41.5 dB at 95 GHz, 21.8–23.5 dB short of the 65 dB requirement; distance alone cannot close that gap on a Ø110 mm disc.

What is measured

  • B, worst single RX port: one RX port with the whole TX beam on, relative to one TX channel's power. The 65 dB requirement applies here.
  • C = B − 19.8 dB: the same port relative to the total TX power (96 channels).
  • All ports: the 96 RX ports together, relative to the total TX power.
  • D: the RX Σ beam output, relative to the total TX power.

TX beams at azimuth −20° (away from RX), 0° and +20° (toward RX). The RX array in this model is the TX tile with 50 Ω ports, not the RX tile.

Remedies to test in CST

Septum to the windowGrounded metal wall on x = 0, up to the window. Cuts the surface path into the facing columns.open
Absorber liningW-band absorber on both septum faces and in the hood. Damps the grazing wave and window reflections.open
Split windowA metal mullion on the septum line, so the window cannot guide power across. A generic radome made the mini model 9.6 dB worse.open
Wider gap, 15–20 mmØ110 mm allows it: a 20 mm gap gives a 79.5 × 46.3 mm plate, 92 mm diagonal. Worth ≈ 11 dB by the fit.open
Tilted windowTilt 5–10° so the specular reflection of the TX beam misses the RX aperture.open
LO-path terminationsEach RX tile's two LO terminations absorb 1.6–3.2× the RX-port power; counted, B gets 4.1–6.2 dB worse. Shield and fence the LO feed.open

Why it matters in this architecture

  • inferenceCompression is not the problem. With ≈ +1.5 dBm per TX tile the worst RX tile sees ≈ −40 dBm, about 19–23 dB below the RX IC's input 1 dB compression point of −17 to −21 dBm.
  • inferenceThe problem is the leakage tone after dechirp. It lands near DC, where the baseband high-pass removes most of it, but its phase-noise skirt (synthesizer noise ×9) spreads over the near range bins and raises the floor.
  • inferenceRange correlation cancels that noise only if TX drive, RX LO and dechirp LO share one synthesizer and matched paths (frequency plan, clocks). Mechanics: radome and sealing; tests: risks.
Details

More results

  • Per-channel C at 95 GHz: −61.5 / −61.3 / −63.0 dB (−20 / 0 / +20°); 8.7–11.9 dB short over 95–99.9 GHz.
  • Worst port in 88–98 GHz: −32.3 dB @ 90.55, −26.4 dB @ 90.80, −35.9 dB @ 90.40 GHz.
  • Under B, 88 / 67 / 80 of the 96 RX tiles are above −65 dB at 95 GHz (boresight / +20° / −20°).
  • Incident versus accepted TX power changes the result by 0.07–0.43 dB at 95–98 GHz.

Convergence caveats

  • The solver stopped at the −20 dB energy limit. Dropping the last 10 % of the record changes the values by up to 1.7 dB (all ports) and 1.8 dB (worst port) at 95–99.9 GHz, 1.7 / 2.1 dB at 89.5–95 GHz, and 11–12 dB below 89.5 GHz.
  • Records end at 0.82 ns (boresight) and 1.04 ns (±20°); RX ringing is still 12.7–18.6 dB below its peak. The 90.8 GHz peak has not settled.
  • The open boundary sits only 1.53–1.6 mm above the patches.
  • Quoted accuracy: ±1 dB at 95 GHz, 1.3–1.6 dB near 99–100 GHz, several dB below 89.5 GHz.
  • Only three TX angles at full size; inside ±10° only boresight. Each further angle is a 2.3–3.9 h twin solve.

X-band board: LMS8001 and LA1214

The X-band disc takes the four quadrant IFs, dechirps them with a copy of the same chirp, and hands four complex beats to the LA1214.

    Velocity ambiguity, digital vs analog dechirp, and the DAC chirp

    Long chirps fold fast targets

    The unambiguous speed is vmax = λ / (4 · Tr): ±7.7 m/s at 100 µs, ±15.4 m/s at 50 µs and ±30.8 m/s at 25 µs (λ 3.075 mm at 97.5 GHz). A road vehicle at 30 m/s needs Tr ≤ 25 µs.

    A 25 µs chirp of 2.5 GHz gives 667 kHz/m, so 150 m is a 100 MHz beat. That does not fit 122.88 Msps complex with guard. Long chirps for range and short chirps for speed pull against each other.

    • inferenceStaggered repetition: alternate two or three Tr values per frame and unfold the speed from the different aliases.
    • inferenceSlope diversity: alternate up and down slopes or two slopes; range–Doppler coupling differs between them and resolves the fold.
    • inferenceTrack-level unwrapping: the tracker predicts the speed and picks the right alias.
    • openThe speed requirement is not written down yet; it decides how much of this is needed.

    Analog dechirp, not digital

    Analog dechirp (this design): the X-band mixer removes the chirp and only the beat, DC to ≈ 50 MHz, reaches the four LS-DCS channels.

    Digital dechirp would sample the full IF: 278–544 MHz of chirp per quadrant, so ≥ 0.6–1.1 Gsps complex per channel. Only the LA1224's two 1.966 Gsps 10-bit converters reach that, and two channels cannot carry four quadrants. Ten bits also leave little room next to the close-in TX leakage.

    Why the DAC chirp is not the main source

    The LA1214 TX DACs could make a baseband chirp, but NXP rates the channel below 140 MHz. After ×9 that is 1.26 GHz at W-band, an 11.9 cm range bin (≈ 3.6 GHz even at the full 491.52 Msps, which NXP does not rate). It also needs an I/Q upconverter at 11 GHz. Keep the DACs for calibration tones, BIST and waveform experiments such as slope diversity. inference

    Two separate synthesizers for TX and RX would let the tiles dechirp to a fixed IF, but their phase noise would not cancel on the TX → RX leakage path. Not recommended. inference

    13 · X-band layer

    One reference for every clock

    One reference on the X-band disc clocks the LA1214 and the chirp synthesizer, and the LA1214 frame timer starts every chirp, so the ramps, the samples and the frames stay locked together.

    reference and sample clocks X-band chirp: LO trees and dechirp copy RAMP trigger and frame SYNC Ethernet with PTP

    122.88 MHzdevice clock family of the LA1214 (30.72–122.88 Msps)

    Three clocks matter for the radar and one for the data link. The device clock sets the ADC sample instants. The synthesizer reference sets the chirp frequency. The RAMP trigger sets when each chirp starts. All three come from one cleaner, so a chirp always begins on the same sample. The PCIe clock only has to meet the PCIe jitter limits; it does not need to be coherent with the radar.

    • inferenceChirp start locked to the ADC sample clock. The RAMP pulse comes from the LA1214 frame timer, and the LMX2595 reference comes from the same cleaner as the LA1214 device clock. Every chirp then starts on the same sample phase, which the Doppler FFT needs.
    • inferenceOne synthesizer for TX, RX LO and dechirp. RFoutA feeds both LO trees; RFoutB is the dechirp copy. The ×9 phase noise term 9 · [φ(t − τ) − φ(t)] then cancels at short delay, which is what the TX → RX leakage path needs. Two synthesizers would share only the reference, and their noise would not cancel.
    • inferenceMatched paths. Keep the TX, RX LO, IF and LO-copy delays close: 1 ns each gives a 1.7 cm range offset, a 1.5 / 1 / 1 / 0.5 ns mismatch gives 10 cm (section 04). Calibrate the rest; matched delays also keep the leakage noise correlated.
    • inferencePhase noise at W-band. Scaling the LMX2595 15 GHz figure to 11 GHz gives about −112.7 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz; ×9 makes it about −93.6 dBc/Hz at 99 GHz.
    • openLMX2595 ramp-trigger pins and the delay from the trigger to the ramp start, with its spread over temperature: datasheet check and a bench measurement.
    • openLA1214 frame timer and GPIO timing: the documentation sits behind an NXP login.

    Why not a 10–60 W GPU module

    The original deck compared three edge-compute options: NVIDIA Jetson Orin for efficiency, Jetson AGX for scale and an AMD APU for general compute confirmed. All three are good parts; none suits this unit.

    • Power. Orin NX runs in 10, 15, 25 and 40 W modes; AGX Orin draws up to 60 W. PoE++ Type 4 leaves ≈ 10.7 W of margin at the nominal load (section 17). A 25–60 W module spends that margin several times over.
    • Heat. The tube is sealed and passively cooled. At 60 W a bare Ø130 × 250 mm body already runs ≈ 36 K above ambient (section 19). Another 10–50 W has nowhere to go.
    • Temperature. One distributor lists AGX Orin at −25…+80 °C, so a −40 °C rating would need a pre-heater. The i.MX 95 has native −40 °C grades.
    • Compute is not the bottleneck. The VSPA array (1.3 TFLOP family peak) does the bulk DSP. The host load is CFAR, angles and tracking: a few GOPS.
    • Cost of the switch. CUDA is lost. OpenCL 3.0 and Vulkan compute on the Mali cover FFT, CFAR and clustering kernels. The Mali is about 30× slower than an Orin-class GPU, which is why the large FFTs stay on the VSPA inference.

    Eight steps take the four receive channels from the converters to a track message; the data rate falls from 62.9 Gb/s to a few Mb/s, and the big drops happen on the LA1214 before anything crosses PCIe.

    FFT loads use 5·N·log₂N operations per transform. The total of 13–27 GFLOP/s is under 3 % of the 1.3 TFLOP family peak of the VSPA array, so even several times the textbook count leaves headroom.

    • confirmedDeck: separate lab transport from product interfaces. Here the product output is the track message; raw or cube streaming is a lab mode on the 10GBASE-T option (section 16).
    • confirmedDeck: make calibration and angle estimation explicit. Step 2 has its own tone injection from the LA1214 TX DACs and per-quadrant tables; the angle is θ = Im(Δ/Σ)/k with the measured slope k (section 09).
    • confirmedDeck: velocity ambiguity is a waveform and algorithm problem. At 100 µs chirps v_max is ±7.7 m/s. Staggered chirp repetition or slope diversity between frames, with unwrapping on the A55, extends it.
    • confirmedDeck: end in a tracker with a defined output message. Step 8 sends a PTP-stamped track list; its fields are sketched in section 16.
    Assumptions, wide mode and timing
    • Frame. 128 chirps × 100 µs = 12.8 ms, so 78 frames and 10 000 chirps per second. A track update can follow every frame; latency is one frame plus processing inference.
    • Velocity. v_max = λ/(4·T) = ±7.7 m/s and Δv = λ/(2·N·T) = 0.12 m/s at λ ≈ 3.1 mm. Shorter chirps raise v_max: ±15.4 m/s at 50 µs, ±30.8 m/s at 25 µs, but the beat for a given range doubles each time.
    • Wide mode. A 4.9 GHz sweep (95–99.9 GHz) gives 327 kHz/m, 32.7 MHz at 100 m, and 3.06 cm bins. A 100 m cube then holds 3268 bins per chirp, ≈ 4.2 Gb/s: still inside one x1 lane, at 65 % of it.
    • Duty. The rates above assume chirps back to back. The blank time between chirps (beam writes, ramp reset) lowers the average, so they are upper bounds.
    • Packing. Samples are 16 + 16 bit complex. Packing to 12 bit cuts the 61.44 Msps raw stream to 5.90 Gb/s, which a single x1 lane carries only without margin.
    • Earlier chain. The original deck put an FPGA for packing and transforms in front of an edge GPU module. Here the VSPA cores do the transforms next to the converters, and the i.MX 95 does only what needs branches and memory: detection, angles and tracks.
    16 · Compute and data

    Interfaces at the rear cap

    Every cable enters through the Ø127 mm rear cap: one M12 X-coded jack carries Ethernet and PoE++, an M12 A-coded jack takes 24/48 V DC, and a capped SMA brings in an external reference; a pressure vent and an earth stud complete the face.

    The original deck drew the boundary between the radar module, the host and the power source as five classes of interface. A sealed tube should carry all five through as few holes as possible. Control, timing and the platform output share one Ethernet link on the X-coded jack, and PoE++ puts power on the same four pairs. High-speed data stays inside the tube on PCIe.

    The PoE++ figure is the IEEE 802.3bt table value confirmed. The protocol choices are this page's proposal; the deck defines the classes, not the wire formats.

    Output message, one per frame

    The tracker ends the pipeline (section 15), so the product output is a short track list. A header carries the unit id, the frame counter, the PTP time of the frame and the waveform in use. Each track then takes 40–64 bytes. At 100 tracks per frame and 78 frames per second that is ≈ 4 Mb/s, which even 1 GbE carries a hundred times over.

    • inferenceIsolation and earth. The PoE PD must stay isolated from the chassis (1500 V class). The earth stud bonds the tube and the cable shields at the cap; the M12 shells bond to the cap, which is the only entry.
    Raw-data mode for lab work

    Calibration, waveform experiments and algorithm work need the samples, not the tracks. With the 10GBASE-T PHY fitted the i.MX 95 forwards what arrives over PCIe to its 10 GbE port, ≈ 9.4 Gb/s of payload. The narrow point is PCIe, not Ethernet. One Gen3 x1 lane (6.3–6.7 Gb/s) carries 4 × 30.72 Msps raw (3.93 Gb/s) or the range-gated cube. Raw samples at 4 × 61.44 Msps (7.86 Gb/s) need both lanes, if the LA1214 can run two links to one host open. The 10GBASE-T PHY draws 2–4 W against 0.5–1 W for 2.5GBASE-T, so raw-data work is best done on the DC input.

    Connector options
    • inferenceReference input. The jitter cleaner takes the SMA reference when it is present and falls back to the internal oscillator. With the dust cap fitted the SMA stays sealed.
    • openDC jack rating. A-coded M12 is rated ≈ 4 A. That covers the nominal 61 W at 24 V (2.5 A) but the 123 W high case only at 48 V (2.6 A); at 24 V it needs 5.1 A. An L-coded M12 (≈ 16 A, 63 V) removes the question.

    17 · Power and mechanics

    Power layer and budget

    The rear disc turns PoE++ or 24/48 V DC into one isolated 12 V bus, every disc makes its own rails from that bus, and the 192 W-band tiles decide whether one PoE cable is enough.

    power12 V intermediate busenable, power-good, PMBushigh-current stages
    60.6 Wnominal input; 30.6 W low, 123.2 W high

    71.3 WPoE++ Type 4 at the PD: 10.7 W margin at nominal
    51 WPoE++ Type 3 at the PD: 9.6 W short at nominal
    12 V bus≈ 5 A between the discs at 60 W

    A 12 V bus keeps the current between the discs near 5 A, and each disc makes its own rails next to its loads. The tile rail is the big one: 24 W at nominal, about 20 A at 1.2 V. Rails that touch the chirp get ultra-low-noise LDOs. The power budget is least certain where it matters most: the tile figures come from published W-band chips, not these ICs, and the LA1214 and LMS8001 have no public power data. Hence three cases.

    Start-up order

    1. Power disc, 12 V bus, PoE class
    2. i.MX 95 boots from the PF09 sequence

    Shutdown runs in reverse. TX bias sits on a Cortex-M7 GPIO for the duty cap and over-temperature trips.

    Design the power disc for PoE++ Type 4 and fit an M12 24/48 V DC input. Type 4 covers the nominal 60.6 W with 10.7 W to spare; the high case of 123 W needs the DC input. Read the negotiated class at start-up and cap the TX duty to it: on Type 3 the nominal case fits only below 44 % duty.

    • speculativeTile power. The 192 tiles are half of the nominal load, and their per-tile power is not measured. Measure one TX and one RX tile first; that number decides which side of the Type 4 line the unit lands on.
    • openLA1214 and LMS8001 power. Not public; 5–15 W together across the cases.
    Input options, example parts, noise and heater
    • inferenceSwitching noise. Keep the converter frequencies and their harmonics out of the beat band (up to ≈ 49 MHz at 122.88 Msps) and the 10.4–11.3 GHz IF band; use spread-spectrum or synchronised converters.
    • inferenceHeater. The 10–20 W window heater runs mainly at cold start, before RF is on. Heater plus electronics must still fit the PD limit.

    IEEE 802.3 asks for the PD to be isolated from earth and chassis, which is why the 12 V stage is an isolated converter. A 24 V-only build can use a plain synchronous buck. The active bridge matters: at about 1.4 A two diode drops of 0.6 V would waste 1.7 W, a sixth of the Type 4 margin.

    18 · Power and mechanics

    Mechanical concept: a round CCTV-style housing

    The radar is packaged like an industrial CCTV tube housing: a standard aluminium tube, a front bezel with the radome window, and a rear cap that carries every connector. Four Ø110 mm discs slide in behind the window, each on its own aluminium spreader and clamp ring, which also carries its heat to the tube wall.

    Shell

    Interactive 3D model of the radar unit: the tube, the four discs and the rear cap. It needs JavaScript; the side section below shows the same stack to scale.

    View

    Drag to turn, Shift-drag to pan, Ctrl + scroll to zoom, double-click to reset; arrow keys, + and − work too. Hover a part for its name; click a part or a number to highlight it. With the shell on, the numbers of the parts inside appear when you pick them in the list below.

    1. : a λ/2 polymer wall (0.92 mm polycarbonate), Ø100 mm, split by a 4 mm metal mullion on the septum line.
    2. : Ø131 × 12 mm; the window sits 1.6 mm back from its face.
    3. : a 1.5 mm open shell over 220° of the top, 35 mm overhang at the front, on two clips.
    4. : 8 × 12 tiles, patch plane 5 mm behind the window.
    5. : 8 × 12 tiles in four 24-tile quadrants.
    6. : a grounded wall between the apertures, from the plate up to the window and the mullion.
    7. : on the back of the W-band disc, with the IF LNAs, the beam CPLD and the 1.2 V POLs.
    8. : 6 blind-mate SMPM (4 IF, dechirp LO, REF in) and a 2 × 30 pin header across the 10 mm gap.
    9. : 4 RF front ends under cans and 2 × LMS8001 (I and Q) with the 90° hybrid on the front; MCU, clock cleaner and OCXO on the back.
    10. : 21 × 21 mm BGA on the back of the X-band disc, on a pedestal of its spreader.
    11. : i.MX 95 (19 × 19 mm), 2 × LPDDR5, eMMC, PF09 PMIC and the Ethernet PHY with magnetics.
    12. : PoE++ PD and its transformer, the isolated 12 V converter, bulk capacitors and the sequencer.
    13. : aluminium plates behind the discs and rings that press them onto the tube wall: the heat path.
    14. : 6061-T6, Ø127 × 6.35 mm wall (ID 114.3 mm), 200 mm long, hard-anodised.
    15. : M12 X-coded Ethernet + PoE++, M12 A-coded 24/48 V DC, SMA REF in with dust cap, ePTFE vent and earth stud.
    16. : saddle clamp at mid-length, a 60 mm arm, a ball joint and a 100 × 100 mm plate.

    CCTV references, assembly and service

    What CCTV tube housings look like

    Common features: extruded or die-cast aluminium, or 304/316L stainless for marine and explosion-proof versions; IP66/IP67 (IEC 60529); IK10 impact (IEC 62262, 20 J); NEMA 4X; a thermostat heater, sometimes a blower; a detachable sunshield; a wall bracket and pole adapter; cable glands or M12 connectors at the rear. confirmed

    Housing typeSizeRating
    Square-section machine-vision housings61–66 mm across, 108–296 mm longIP66/IP67
    Explosion-proof stainless bullet housings≈ 105 mm ID × 330 mm, 73 mm windowIP68
    Box housings90 mm inside widthIP67, IK10, heater to −40 °C
    Extruded anodised aluminium tubes200–350 mm longIP67, sunshield and heater options
    Large outdoor cameras464 × 183 × 183 mm, 3.2 kgIK10, IP66, NEMA 4X

    A Ø110–130 mm tube, 200–300 mm long, sits squarely in the normal CCTV size range, so brackets, sunshields and vents can be standard parts. inference

    Assembly order

    1. Build each disc with its spreader and clamp ring and test it on the bench (W-band: LO level at the tiles and TX output; X-band: dechirp on all four channels).
    2. Fit the M12 jacks, the SMA, the vent and the earth stud to the rear cap, with the harness to the power disc.
    3. Join the power, compute and X-band discs on their headers and the mezzanine, slide them in from the front and expand the clamp rings against the wall.
    4. Fit the W-band disc last: the five SMPM bullets blind-mate into the X-band disc. Check the patch-plane depth from the tube face.
    5. Fit the septum, then the bezel with the window and the heater ring; the mullion lands on the septum line.
    6. Close the rear cap, pressure-test the sealed tube, then fit the ePTFE vent and the desiccant.

    Service

    • The rear cap opens without touching the RF stack; the service loop lets it swing clear.
    • The bezel and window come off from the front, and the W-band disc slides out after them.
    • One cable entry and metal all round: the tube stays a continuous shield.

    The clamp rings are drawn as expanding split rings with wedge screws; a press fit would work too but makes the stack hard to remove. speculative

    19 · Power and mechanics

    Radome, heat and sealing

    Three things decide whether the tube works outdoors: a window that passes 95–99.9 GHz and survives impact, a heat path that gets about 60 W out through the wall, and seals that keep water off the window and out of the tube.

    0.92 mmλ/2 polycarbonate window; |S11| ≤ −27 dB over 95–99.9 GHz

    5–7 Krise inside the tube, tiles to wall
    +42 Ktube surface over ambient, bare Ø127 × 200 mm at 60 W
    +26 Kthe same with the finned Ø160 × 300 mm body
    10–20 Wbezel heater for a −40 °C start and de-icing

    Window: a half-wave wall

    A wall half a wavelength thick inside the material reflects least: t = λ0/(2√εr), λ0 = 3.075 mm at 97.5 GHz. At that thickness every material below stays at |S11| ≤ −27 dB over 95–99.9 GHz, so the window does not limit the band; what it does reflect goes back towards the RX aperture.

    • openShape. Flat, or a very shallow dome (radius ≥ 300 mm) to shed water. A flat window tilted 5–10° in an angled bezel sends the specular TX reflection away from the RX aperture. Both need CST.
    • inferenceSplit window. Two halves with a metal mullion on the septum line, so the window cannot guide TX energy across to the RX aperture.
    • openWater and ice. A water film costs heavy loss at W-band. Use a hydrophobic coating and the heated bezel ring, and measure the loss wet.
    • openHeater wires. Wires across the aperture must run perpendicular to the E-field. The tile polarisation is not documented yet, so the wire direction waits for it.

    Heat path

    The flip-chipped tile ICs send their 24 W down through the bumps into the PCB, then through a spreader and a clamp ring to the tube wall; the big step is from the tube to the air.

    Hot climates: at 60 W and +55 °C the bare Ø127 × 200 mm tube puts the W-band disc near 103 °C, too close to the i.MX 95's 105 °C junction limit. Use the finned Ø160 × 300 mm body, hold dissipation to 30–40 W by TX duty cycling, or rate the unit for +45 °C. CFD and a chamber test settle it. open

    Sealing and environment

    • inferenceO-rings in the bezel's rear face and at the rear cap; the window gasketed behind the bezel lip. Target IP66 and IP67; IP68 only after a test.
    • inferenceBreathing: an ePTFE vent on the rear cap plus desiccant, so day–night swings do not pump moist air in.
    • inferenceHeater: 10–20 W on the bezel ring for the −40 °C start and de-icing, as in CCTV housings.
    • inferenceShielding and entry: conductive gaskets at both caps; every cable enters at the rear cap.
    • openTests: IP66/IP67 spray and immersion, a pressure-decay leak test, the window's impact rating.

    Mechanics for isolation

    The worst RX port sits at −41.5 dB against a 65 dB requirement (section 10), and a generic radome made it 9.6 dB worse on the mini model. The housing adds a septum up to the window, a split window, absorber and room for a wider gap; each needs a full-size CST run. open

    Isolation features in the housing
    Septum to the windowA grounded 4 mm wall from the ground plate up to the window, sealed into a groove with a conductive or absorbing gasket, absorber on both faces. open
    Split window and mullionTwo windows with a metal bar on the septum line, so no wave travels inside the window from TX to RX. open
    Wider gapØ110 allows 15–20 mm instead of 5 mm (20 mm: plate 79.5 × 46.3 mm, 92 mm diagonal, 9 mm corner clearance). Today the septum and absorber fill the 5 mm gap. inference
    Absorber frame and hood liningAround each aperture and under the front of the sunshield, where the grating lobes near ±50° at ±10° scan land. open
    Tilted window5–10° of tilt steers the window's specular TX reflection away from the RX aperture. open
    Not distance aloneCoupling falls about 25 dB per decade of spacing; 23 dB more needs about 8.5× the spacing, roughly 70 mm, which does not fit. inference
    Details

    Thicker walls

    • Full-wave walls (2 × λ/2): HDPE 2.03 mm −23.3 / −23.6 dB, polycarbonate 1.84 mm −21.5 / −21.8 dB at 95 / 99.9 GHz.
    • 1.5λ polycarbonate (2.76 mm): −18.1 / −18.5 dB, 0.37 dB one way; 2λ (3.68 mm): −15.9 / −16.2 dB, 0.49 dB, at tanδ 0.008.
    • Loss grows with thickness and tanδ; the band-edge reflection grows with the number of half-waves, because the wall is matched at 97.5 GHz only.
    • The εr 3.0 wall of the CST model has σ = 0.163 S/m, which is tanδ ≈ 0.010 at 95 GHz.

    Hood geometry

    The sunshield (R 70 mm, 35 mm ahead of the bezel, over 220° of the top) clears about 49° upward and 44° sideways from the aperture edges. The ±10° scan region and most of the 47° tile beam pass; the grating lobes near ±50° graze it, hence the absorber. inference

    Thermal steps, inside

    • PCB via farm: 1.15 W/cm² through 2.0 mm at k_eff ≈ 10 W/m·K is about 2.3 K (2 K for a 1.6 mm board).
    • Spreader: 2–3 K over a mean path of about 20 mm to the rim (estimated for 5 mm; 6 mm is drawn).
    • Clamp ring with a 0.5 mm gap pad at 3 W/m·K: 1–2 K.
    • The LA1214 and the i.MX 95 sit on pedestals of their own spreaders; keep the hot ICs near the rim side.

    Outside

    • Correlations: natural convection on a horizontal cylinder, grey-body radiation ε = 0.85, still air at +55 °C.
    • Sun: 1000 W/m² on 0.0325 m² of projected area at an absorptivity of 0.3–0.5 adds 10–16 W.
    • At 60 W and +55 °C a Ø130 mm shell reaches about 90–105 °C.
    20 · Plan and evidence

    Main risks, and the test that settles each

    Eight risks are open, six from the design deck and two from this work; the chart places each one’s first evidence and its settling test on the development phases of section 21.

    8 openrisks: six from the deck, two new
    21.8–23.5 dBisolation short of 65 dB at 95 GHz
    95–97.5 GHzwhere array, TX IC and RX IC all work
    +42 Kbare Ø127 × 200 mm tube over ambient at 60 W
    R1 · from the deck

    Band alignment

    Array 95–99.9 GHz; TX IC peak +1.6 dBm near 94.5 GHz; RX IC gain 17 dB at 93 GHz, 10 dB at 97.5 GHz. All three overlap only at ≈ 95–97.5 GHz.

    TestA 2 × 2 tile board on the LMX2595: TX power, RX gain and NF from 94 to 100 GHz.

    Done whenThe chirp band is frozen on measured curves: 95–97.5 GHz, or wider if the link closes.

    See 04 Frequency plan

    R2 · from the deck

    Scan margin

    At 3.30 mm the ±10° grating lobes are −10.7 to −13.6 dB at 95 GHz but −6.2 dB at 98 GHz. ±20° fails; no diagonals were simulated.

    TestFull-wave CST of a 2.90 mm or checkerboard 8 × 12 with diagonal scans; a range scan of the first disc.

    Done whenThe worst lobe in the ±10° cone is −10 dB or lower over the chirp band.

    See 08 Scan range

    R3 · from the deck

    TX → RX isolation

    Worst RX port −41.5 dB at 95 GHz: 21.8–23.5 dB short of 65 dB. Two facing RX columns take 69–90 % of it; a radome made it 9.6 dB worse.

    TestFull-size CST twin with septum, absorber, split window and 15–20 mm gap; dechirped RX spectrum with TX on.

    Done whenCoupling is −65 dB per channel or lower with the window fitted, or the link budget accepts the measured floor.

    See 10 Isolation

    R4 · from the deck

    Velocity ambiguity

    v_max = λ/(4·T_r) is ±7.7 m/s at 100 µs and ±30.8 m/s at 25 µs. Short chirps raise beat and data rate. The required speed span is not stated.

    TestSimulate staggered intervals and slope diversity; track a reflector moving faster than v_max.

    Done whenThe tracker reports the true radial speed at 2–3× v_max, with no folded tracks.

    See 12 Chirp and timing

    R5 · from the deck

    Thermal margin

    60.6 W nominal input; 24 W of it in the tiles (≈ 1.15 W/cm²). The bare Ø127 × 200 mm tube runs ≈ +42 K at 60 W; a finned Ø160 × 300 mm body ≈ +26 K (section 19).

    TestResistors at the tile, LA1214 and i.MX 95 positions in the real tube; +55 °C chamber with a solar lamp.

    Done whenEvery die stays below its junction limit at rated ambient; body and TX duty cap are fixed.

    See 19 Radome and heat

    R6 · from the deck

    Manufacturability

    192 flip-chip tiles at 3.30 mm. CST tiles touch; real ones need 50–100 µm gaps. LO paths match within 1 mm. The CST tile has a 30 µm air layer.

    Test2 × 2 and 4 × 4 tile coupons: X-ray, gain and phase spread; one CST tile re-run with resin.

    Done whenThe tile spread fits the IC trim range and the coupon yield is known.

    See 06 Tile in 3D

    R7 · new in this work

    LMS8001 at 11 GHz

    The LMS8001B is sold “up to 12 GHz” but characterised at 5–6 GHz. Its PLL stops at 9.5 GHz, so 11 GHz needs EXTLO, whose limit is not stated.

    TestThe companion board with an 11 GHz EXTLO balun: gain, NF, IIP3, I/Q balance, next to an HMC1056.

    Done whenOne dechirp mixer is chosen on measured data; the HMC1056 footprint stays until then.

    See 11 X-band board

    R8 · new in this work

    LA1214 for an i.MX host

    LA1214 power, ADC range and sync are not public. Its host software targets Layerscape; nothing public shows an i.MX 95 host.

    TestAn LA1224 reference board on an i.MX 95 over PCIe Gen3 x1: firmware load, VSPA FFT, DMA, power.

    Done when4 channels at 30.72 Msps stream for hours without loss within 7 W, or the LA9310 replaces it.

    See 14 Processor

    More numbers behind each risk

    Per risk

    • confirmedR1 The TX IC LO input is specified at 10–11 GHz, i.e. 90–99 GHz after ×9; 99.9 GHz needs an 11.1 GHz drive.
    • openR1 The “7 GHz 3-dB BW” label on the TX IC plot does not match its markers: they sit 5.6 GHz apart at W-band, 4.35 dB below the peak.
    • confirmedR2 El −10° lobe by frequency: −9.2 dB (88), −7.3 (90), −10.7 (95), −6.2 dB (98 GHz). Worst ±20° lobe −1.1 dB.
    • confirmedR2 Pitch study (8 × 8, array factor): 2.90 mm gives −11.6 dB in the ±10° box at 95 GHz, −12.2 dB with a checkerboard.
    • inferenceR3 Leakage of ≈ −40 dBm per RX tile is 20–24 dB below IP1dB: the cost is the leakage tone and ×9 phase noise after dechirp, not compression.
    • inferenceR3 Distance alone would need ≈ 8.5× the 8.3 mm port-column spacing, which does not fit a Ø110 mm disc.
    • inferenceR4 2.5 GHz in 100 µs gives 166.7 kHz/m (25 MHz at 150 m); halving T_r doubles both the beat and v_max.
    • inferenceR5 At +55 °C ambient a Ø130 mm shell at 60 W reaches ≈ 90–105 °C, against the 105 °C junction limit of the industrial i.MX 95.
    • inferenceR5 A finned Ø160 × 300 mm body runs ≈ +26 K at 60 W; 30–40 W of dissipation (TX duty) also works.
    • inferenceR6 0.05 mm of stripline is already 10° at 97 GHz after ×9; 1 mm of mismatch is ≈ 10° across a 4.9 GHz chirp that calibration cannot remove.
    • confirmedR7 Above a 4.8 GHz LO each LMS8001 channel has only 0° or 180°; Lime has never tested a DC IF.
    • confirmedR7 The companion board’s EXTLO balun covers 4.5–3500 MHz, so it needs rework before an 11 GHz test.
    • confirmedR8 The LA12xx data sheets sit behind an NXP login; so the power budget carries the LA1214 at 4 / 7 / 12 W until NXP gives a number.
    • confirmedR8 Fallback LA9310: 5 RX + 1 TX at 153 Msps, 1.5 W, one PCIe Gen3 lane, documents without NDA.

    Gaps that are decisions, not risks

    • confirmedMonopulse: 0.2° at SNR 16 dB is not met by 8 × 12 (0.32° el, 0.47° az). It needs ≈ 1.6× the elevation and 2.35× the azimuth aperture, or 20.0 / 23.3 dB of SNR. 09 Monopulse
    • inferencePower: PoE++ Type 4 (71.3 W at the PD) covers the nominal 60.6 W, not the 123.2 W high case. Cap TX duty by the negotiated class and keep a 24/48 V DC input. 17 Power
    • speculativeTile power: 80–300 mW per TX tile and 50–200 mW per RX tile come from published W-band chips, not from these ICs. Measure first; it moves R5 and the PoE class.

    Smaller open items

    • openPhase-bit count, register map and BIT(2:1) meaning of the tile ICs; RX IC LO level and supply power.
    • openLMX2595 VCO core edges near 10.5–11.1 GHz and the calibration-free ramp span.
    • openM12 X-coded contact rating for Type 4 current at the internal temperature; PF09 production status.
    • openWater film on the window at W-band; heater wires must run along x, across the E-field (co-pol E is along y in the CST tile).
    21 · Plan and evidence

    Build and validation sequence

    Six phases without dates, as in the design deck; each phase ends on a gate that names a number measured on this design, and settles the risks of section 20 in the order shown.

    what the phase buildsexit gaterisk settled (links to its card)

    Every phase that builds hardware runs the deck’s build flow for its own scope, with a gate between steps; the pilot build runs all of it at batch size.

    1. Silicon and RF die: the TX and RX ICs, as supplied
    2. Packaging: the 3.30 mm tile, flip chip and BGA
    3. Board build: four Ø110 mm discs
    4. Module test: tile coupon, then each disc
    5. System integration: the stack in the tube
    6. Qualification: heat, sealing, EMC, power

    Phase by phase: entry, work and exit
    Phase 1

    Architecture freeze

    EntryThis page and the full-wave CST runs of the 3.30 mm 8 × 12 array and the twin model

    • CST: 2.90 mm and checkerboard arrays with diagonal scans
    • CST: full-size twin with septum, radome and a 15–20 mm gap; one tile with resin in the air layer
    • vendor answers: LA1214 data sheet, LMS8001 EXTLO limit, tile-IC phase bits and RX supply
    • board-to-board interfaces and the EMC and qualification plan written down

    Done whenChirp band candidates, pitch, X-band parts and disc interfaces are frozen on paper

    Phase 2

    RF module validation

    EntryFrozen candidates; layouts of the 2 × 2 tile board, one LO column and the tile coupons

    • TX output, RX gain and NF, LO level and tile current on the 2 × 2 board
    • chirp ramp and dechirp mixer benches
    • LA1224 reference board on an i.MX 95 board

    Done whenLO ≥ +5 dBm at every tile pin over the chirp band, TX and RX measured 94–100 GHz, one mixer and one synthesizer chosen, and the chirp band frozen

    Phase 3

    Board integration

    EntryPhase 2 numbers inside their targets

    • first W-band disc with 192 tiles, the X-band, compute and power discs
    • discs cabled on the bench; beam tables loaded through the CPLD
    • far-field range scan of the W-band disc

    Done whenEvery tile answers on the beam bus, the ±10° scan meets −10 dB, and 4 channels stream to the i.MX 95 for hours with no loss

    Phase 4

    System integration

    EntryEach disc passes its own test

    • the stack in the tube with window, septum and absorber
    • quadrant calibration with the LA1214 DAC tone and a boresight source
    • moving-target and corner-reflector runs

    Done whenLeakage after dechirp fits the link budget, Σ/Δ channels match to ≤ 0.25 dB / 2°, tracks beyond v_max are correct and leave over Ethernet with PTP time

    Phase 5

    Qualification

    EntryA frozen unit design

    • +55 °C chamber with solar load and −40 °C cold start with the heater
    • IP66 / IP67, EMC, vibration
    • PoE Type 3 and Type 4 and the 24/48 V DC input

    Done whenJunction limits hold at the rated ambient, IP and EMC pass, and the power cap follows the PoE class

    Phase 6

    Pilot build

    EntryThe qualified design with build and calibration documents

    • a small batch through the full build flow
    • a production calibration station
    • yield tracking per tile, disc and unit

    Done whenTile and disc yield and the calibration time per unit are known, and units match the reference unit

    Design rules from the deck that shape the plan

    • confirmedGate discipline: no step starts before the one before it passes (deck build flow).
    • confirmedModular test points and design for assembly and calibration (deck module topology).
    • confirmedEMC and qualification planned from architecture freeze, not after it (deck mechanics slide).
    • inferencePhase 2 carries most of the early risk: four of the eight risks get their first hardware number there, so its boards come first.
